name: Yiddish
catalog_quote: 2.3.2 Word stress. Word stress (usually high in isolation) is bound to the root syllable, which is most frequently the first. ... Each rhythmic unit (e.g. phrase, sentence) has one and only one high. ... The major constraint is that the high stress be selected from a syllable that can bear word stress when that word is uttered in isolation.
sweep_summary: Only one title-hit for Eastern Yiddish: Green 2008, 'The Infix [-ev-] and Initial Accent in Yiddish Verbs' (EYDES volume, Niemeyer/de Gruyter, pp. 83-96, doi:10.1515/9783484970632.83). It is squarely about accent placement in a Yiddish verb class but is paywalled: Semantic Scholar marks it CLOSED with the abstract withheld; de Gruyter serves a bot-challenge; not on archive.org or HathiTrust. Priority medium (dedicated stress paper, but a verb-class study unlikely to overturn the stratum-based coding). Nothing new read contradicts the catalog: Katz 1993 p. 49 (open author scan, held by the project) restates the catalog's deciding analysis (Germanic component root-bound stress, Semitic component penultimate with shift under suffixation) and confirms the 'lexical' coding; Jacobs 2005 §4.5.1 snippets add that penultimate is the language-wide default with the Germanic component root-initial and name Weinreich 1954, Wolf 1977 and Glasser 1990 as the main treatments (Jacobs 2005 and Weinreich 1954 remain the high-priority unread items on the existing list of works to obtain).org, HathiTrust and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: To cite one pervasive contrast, the Germanic component has root-bound stress and, consequently, fixed full and reduced vowels, e.g., Northeastern Yiddish /eb "(I) live," /ébn "life," lébadik "lively", lébadika "(pl.) lively," lébadikorhéjt "during his/her lifetime." Even when the stem loses primary stress in deference to a stressed suffix (as in the last cited item), it retains stress and vowel color vis-a-vis the post-tonic vowel [...] Semitic component items, by contrast, exhibit penultimate stress. Suffixation results in shift of stress to the newly penultimate syllable [...] Stress is boundary linked, as in classical Hebrew, although penultimate rather than ultimate
new_statements.citation: Katz, Dovid (1993). The Phonology of Ashkenazic. In Lewis Glinert (ed.), Hebrew in Ashkenaz: A Language in Exile, 46-87. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 49, section 'Coexisting Phonologies within Yiddish' (PDF pp. 8-9)
new_statements.reading: Two coexisting stress subsystems keyed to lexical stratum: Germanic-component words carry fixed root-bound stress (usually the first syllable) that does not move under affixation; Semitic-component words carry penultimate stress that shifts rightward under suffixation. Stress placement therefore depends on which stratum a word belongs to, which is what the catalog's 'lexical' coding encodes.

sources.quote: To cite one pervasive contrast, the Germanic component has root-bound stress and, consequently, fixed full and reduced vowels, e.g., Northeastern Yiddish /eb "(I) live," /ébn "life," lébadik "lively", lébadika "(pl.) lively," lébadikorhéjt "during his/her lifetime." [...] Semitic component items, by contrast, exhibit penultimate stress. Suffixation results in shift of stress to the newly penultimate syllable and in the transformation of shewa to a full vowel [...] Stress is boundary linked, as in classical Hebrew, although penultimate rather than ultimate (scanned; '/eb' = léb, '/ébn' = lébn)
sources.locator: printed p. 49, section 'Coexisting Phonologies within Yiddish' (PDF pp. 8-9, duplicate scans of p. 49)
sources.note: Restates the two-stratum analysis of the catalog source: Germanic-component words have root-bound stress that stays on the root under suffixation (léb, lébn, lébedik, lébedikerhéyt); Semitic-component words have penultimate stress that shifts to the new penult under suffixation (málbesh ~ malbúshim), 'boundary linked.. although penultimate rather than ultimate'. Same author as the catalog's deciding source (Katz 1987); confirms the stratum-conditioned ('lexical') coding.
